segments.description: Justin, it's great to have you here. Many in the conference will know you from your work developing some of Britain's top players, including Jack Draper and Joe Salisbury. I actually remember Jack from the early days. I was working with the LTA talent ID team when he was about nine or 10 years old, and even back then he stood out as one of the most skilled and fiercely competitive kids in those camps. It's been incredible to see how far he's come and how your work has helped shape both his and Joe's career. Today I just wanted to explore the coaching philosophies and practical lessons behind their journeys and what other coaches can take away from that experience. So the first question I have for you is developing distinct identities in singles and doubles. So you've worked closely with both Jack Draper and Joe Salisbury, two very different players in both personality and pathway. From your experience, what are the key developmental differences between building a top singles player versus a world-class double specialist, and how do you identify where players' real potential lies early on? Yeah, it's an interesting question because in hindsight, where they both sit in their careers right now, you'd have thought that there was a distinct difference. But looking back, all you're looking for is that the relationship and the spark between you and a player where you've got a real love for coaching and they've got a real love for the sport that they've been introduced to.

And so there's like a kindred spirit where you both, I think that's why there's a lot of fortune, there's a lot of luck. Yeah, you have to have a bit of magic between you and the player whereby the player is sort of secretly saying to you, like, I'm really into this, you know, are you? And you're going, I'm really into this, are you? And then your journey starts and I was, you know, back when I was coaching both of them when they were young, it was all about, first of all, it was all about tools, tools in the tool kit, tools in the toolbox. And I know that we want to, you know, there's lots of expressions out there like, you know, make sure you water all the flowers in the garden, make sure everything gets looked at. But I really did feel that my responsibility when I had them, you know, starting with Joe when he was sort of five or six and starting with Jack at a similar age, it's a bit of a no-brainer really. You're going to have to teach them pretty much from carte blanche, you've got a blank page. And so teaching the skills and so my, you know, you ask me these questions, you know, has made me really look at what really was my philosophy and it was very, very game orientated. And it wasn't because it was fashionable, it wasn't because I felt like it was the right thing to do and it may not have been terribly fashionable, but I know a lot of things, you know, that we teach can be trendy or you look on YouTube nowadays or, you know, Instagram and you think, oh, I'll do that today.

But my idea was, well, hold on a second, these kids don't even know the game yet. So let's share with them the game, let's introduce all the different aspects to the game, the five game playing situations or whatever you want to call it and all the skills that are necessary. And the nice thing about them catching me at the right time in my career was, you know, I was young, I was strong, which is important because if you're strong and you're fit and you see physicality as part of the game, then that's how you're going to teach. You're going to teach from a basis of physicality. And, you know, and I never say this because I'm trying to big myself up at all, but I loved martial arts and boxing and kickboxing from an early age. And I think I always used to think, well, if I can't be a professional kickboxer, if I can't be a tie boxer because I want to go to work every day and be able to walk, how can I introduce my passion for physicality? And because I also played tennis, I thought, God, there's such a synergy between these individual sports mentally. So I know that if you spoke to either of the boys, they'd say, and anyone that I've coached, they'd always say, oh, does he talk about boxing all the time? I say, yeah, I did. Because from a physicality perspective, it's very similar with the rotation, the way the powers developed with some of the soft skills that you need. And I was on court only yesterday, you know, doing a little jab in and out, show my player how boxes have to create space.

You know, there's no two balls that come at you the same. So you've got to be ready to read that ball. And this would have been the language that I would have had throughout the whole time of coaching them. In fact, you know, not so much with Jack, but Joe ended up being a very good, a very good kickboxer because our warmup would be with the pads. Look, I was training last night. Come on, let's do some. Because all the time I was training, I was thinking, boy, this is so useful. Tennis is often described as a one-legged sport. We do so many things off one leg. But actually, if you want power, you need to be sort of sat down and grounded. So there's so many sort of physical literacies that you can get if you find a sport like, you know, like martial arts. And I say to anybody out there, one of the big things is if you're wondering what you can do to help your player physically and you, because again, there's lots of different exercises. I go out on the tour and I see all the different nations doing different things, all the different coaches doing different exercises. But I suppose if I was starting someone right now and I am, you know, and I've already spoken to a 10-year-old girl's dad, I said, please get her involved in kickboxing. Oh, she loves that. She thinks it's wonderful. I say it's so good for your hand-eye coordination, your foot-eye coordination, your distance, your spacing, and you're in a gym.

So the environment is, I know there's a lot of love in the gym, but it's also a pretty tough place to operate. You know, and you've got to be a killer. And that's sort of the unspoken characteristic that you need to have as a player is that you need to be a killer. And when you talk about Jack and Joe being different, yeah, different personalities, but innately connected through their desire to want to win. And that's where I came in because I said, another one of our secret chats, are you want to win? Oh, really? Who wants to win more? Me or you? Oh, we'll see. And that's where you can have a little bit of fun in your sessions. So whatever game you're playing, okay. So open-face racket skills in both boxes will play and most coaches will play, but will you play until one of you collapses? I doubt it. Will one of you play until one of you gets a 10-point lead? I doubt it. And will the other one try and stop the other one from getting a 10-point lead? I doubt it. So what I'm saying is if you want to be a killer coach as well, you've got to understand the rules, understand your topic, understand the narrative, understand what it is you've got to deliver, but deliver it in the context of reality. Deliver it in the context. I can't imagine somebody going in and, let's say, fighting Mike Tyson back in the day. And the coach would say, oh, just use your jab and stay away from his right hand.

I think they'd say, hold on just a second. Hold on just a second. You're in with a savage killer. And I think a little bit sometimes, you know, when we go on call, even now as a pro coach, when I'm out there, I'll be in Vienna, surely, and then cheer in ATP tour finals, I talk quite a lot about, you know, the physicality and the characteristics of who we're playing. Gronola's, Zabayos, you know, those boys, when we play them at doubles, we know they're going to fight to the death. We know that I can, because I can hear it in the way they celebrate. I can see it in Gronola's eyes. And you can see it in certain sports when you can see in Harry Kane, when he's about to score his umpteenth goal for England. There's a difference between killers and guys that are just out there getting it done. And I think any sport where you can find an individualness like Rory McElroy, the Masters, I mean, come on. Great example. Come on. Great example. The adversity that he was under, yeah. I get the opportunity at five years old, six years old, to create the mould. So every conversation that you have, every lesson that you have, every interaction that you have with parents, every moment, every game that you play is not just a game, it's a game to the death in the context of our sport. So I hope that gives you a little introduction, but both boys very, very similar in that they've got that under the skin, under the surface.

And what a privilege it is to be a coach, right? Like to have that chance to be able to influence like that. And actually, I agree 100% what you're saying, it's tennis is like a combat sport with two rackets instead of your fist, right? It's just the same thing. And like, how many people do you meet that are really willing to fight and actually want, you know, when I say like a competitive person, they love the battle, they don't want to love and love when they want, they want someone to hang in there with them. They want them to fight back with them. You know, um, yeah, that's, that's awesome. I mean, that's incredibly great. I mean, I've got a second question for you and hopefully a third. It feels a bit like what's that show when you sit in the chair and you have to answer the questions. Mastermind or something. Mastermind. Well, you kind of are mastermind. So it kind of fits. Come on, let's do it. The question I've got is a trend, the sort of transition and resilience and development. So you talk a lot about, you know, that fight, but what about the resilience to keep going? So for example, correct me if I'm wrong, but Jack seemed to face a chef, share a physical setbacks early in his career. While Joe's rise came later through persistence and a shift towards the doubles. What did you focus on as a coach to help each of them navigate through transitional phases, whether it was from junior to pro or frustration to stability?

And how can coaches best support players through these moments? Yeah, well, I mean, I stopped coaching Jack when he was 16. So we had just come back from India. He'd reached 75 in the world ITF at 15. And the goal was to break the goal was to break top 100. So when you're dealing with a mentality like Jack Draper, he will only see himself as as aiming for the top. So in terms of mentality, when you when you find yourself in the company of somebody that they already sees themselves. And this is a long, long before the days of and the words like manifestation, which I truly believe in because I think that, you know, someone like Jack and Joe, they've been there, they've been the recipients of manifestation, whether they know it or not. But the people around them, the guys in their stable, the guys in their crew, the family members, you're all part of setting standards. And I know setting standards is a, you know, an important sort of phrase and it can go over some coaches heads. But who you hang out with, who you mix with is going to create your mentality. So Jack, you know, the idea was for Jack to go to India. We went over to India to play these ITFs and they were tough. They were tough. The tournaments were tough. And but the whole conversation was around, mate, one more match. Come on, come on, give me one more set. Come on, give me one more day of hard work. And it was brutal when he got those injuries.

And and that's where you sort of find out where your bond is between you and a player as well, because the player is not going to make it unless you squeeze a little bit. But if you break them, then that's not very good either. So you've got you've got to tread such a fine balance between, I think someone said, and I've always used it. It's like a wet bar of soap. If you squeeze too hard, it pops out the top. And if you don't squeeze enough, you lose it at the bottom. So you've got to keep jiggling, jiggling, jiggling this thing along and hustling and hustling. So everyone who thinks that it's just going to be a fun journey and a fun circus is pretty brutal because these are the these are the sort of the stories and the impacts and the scar tissue that you create when you're young. That then comes back. And obviously, you know, Jack's had some troubles with, you know, but he grew a little bit late. Same as Joe, they grow late. Joe had to, you know, Joe's poor Joe's junior career was curtailed through glandular fever. I mean, so bad. I mean, but if it wasn't for glandular fever, he may not have focused on doubles because he was pretty much told, you know, you carry on training like a singles player, your body's going to body's going to say no, thanks, can't do this. And his body kept breaking down. So, you know, he went off to Memphis University. We sort of said goodbye for a few years, stayed in touch.

And he trained hard and he grew so much. I mean, he grew so much. And, you know, when you grow so much, it puts another strain on the body. So he wasn't one of these sort of slow, slow, easy, steady growers. And I know that Jack was the same. So, you know, then you get into, you're playing pro tennis, but your body says, hold on a sec. I'm not a pro. I can't cut with all these rigors. So you're pretty much then you're back to your base level of psychology, your base level of toughness. And poor Jack's got to deal with that right now in the fact that he's had to curtail his season again, you know, finish his season early with the bruising on that left arm. And he's going to have to show how tough he is. But all that toughness has been sort of instilled in a wrap around tennis love. There's a lot of, you know, when you're engaged with these players, you know, there's a lot of tennis love. And I'll let you know, let you guys into, you know, the big, the big secret for me in my brain is that one day when I write my book, it'll be called tough love and the love and the love. Of course, the love pertains to tennis, but that's what it feels like it is. If you don't teach, if you don't teach toughness, then you're never going to make it. And if you don't teach love for yourself, you're never going to make it either. And I think what I find interesting now is listening to the pros talk and there seems to be a real conversation out there right now about mental health and about how, you know, how brutal the tour is.

So you're teaching, you're teaching on the one hand, you're teaching this wonderful passion. It's a game for life. You're going to love it. It's wonderful. But at the top end, you know, you're teaching them to go to parts of the world where the temperatures are going to almost kill you, you know, in a sort of tennis sense. You're going to be struggling on the road for 35, 40 weeks of the year. You're barely going to see your family unless you can afford to have them travel with you. So, you know, you've got to be realistic. And I love the fact that I'm still with Joe now after all this time from five or six years old to sort of 33. He'll be going off to cheer in and what a blessing. What an absolute gift. And I think we're at the stage in his career. I say we're at the stage in his career because I feel like I've been part of it where we're just so like grateful and so happy to be at a great tennis event again. And there's perspective. And I think you can hear like Sabalenka talk about trying to find perspective with craving. We're chasing. What do we want? We want these wins. We want these victories. We want these trophies, you know, being with hanging out with Jack in Indian Wells this year was such a privilege. You know, I'm not part of his coaching team, but whenever I'm around, he says, just you get in my box now. You get in there. Don't you move? You know, so I think there is a real connection between us because that's just, that's just, you know, that's just the time that we spent together.

But once the trophy had been lifted and once the confetti has fallen, you're off to the next tournament and he has little time to celebrate. And then he's packing for Miami and then you get a real sense of now we move to Miami with all that pressure and expectation. And you know, and then he loses his first round in Miami and you go, well, you know, that's the brutality and what does that do inside your brain? So if you don't teach yourself compassion, if you don't have love for yourself and perspective, then I think it's a rough, it's a rough ride. And sometimes the last thing I tell Joe before he goes out is, I love you, but you're a great guy. You get out there and do your best because that's all we can ever do. That's, that's amazing. I mean, I just think it's, you know, I mean, again, I love the tough, but you call it tough love. Tough love. Yeah. Tough love. Because there is that balance as well, isn't there? Like you're saying, going too far using the soap analogy. I wonder how many people go too far, but equally how many people don't, don't push enough and not really understand what, what being pushy is. You know, because the idea of being pushy is not a good thing, right? Like it's generally seen as quite a negative, negative. Well, wonderful. The wonderful thing is, and I hope that I get enough of an opportunity to now teach this because I now have a reputation at my center and in the county for doing something which,

I heard from a, a good friend of mine who'd said, who saw, who's that wonderful coach in California that coached all the Pete Sampras, Tracy Austin, wonderful coach, Lindsay Davenport. He's an old gruff guy. Oh, he passed away this year. Pete, I can't remember his name. Hopefully, hopefully it'll come to one of us anyway. But, but what I found myself developing this little glint in my eye. I can't think of that. There's Peter though, right? I can't remember. It's wonderful. But, but the idea is that there's, there's a glint in your eye. So when you say things like, I've got a couple of players that I'm working with now. And I said, and I woke up and I just tapped them on a shoulder and I say, you'd, yeah, great to see you today. Great warm up. Wonderful. You do know that toss won't be good enough. You do know that. And they'll go, oh my God, what do you mean? I can see the shock a little bit, a little bit of shock. And I go, well, that toss, because everyone that I've ever seen, and I can show you right now, a hundred players. In fact, you picked the player. I'll show you, we'll see where the toss is, shall we? And they go, all right. And I go, oh, just, I just don't want you to waste your time practicing the wrong toss anyway. I'll stand over here and watch you again and see how much you care about it. So there's always like a, a little hug, a little dig in the ribs, a little, a little tap on the back.

I'm with you. A little poke in the solar plexus. So you're a little bit with them, but you're only with them if we're on the same page. Yeah. And if are you taking responsibility for your ball toss? If you're not taking responsibility for your ball toss, and I'm going to have to teach you your ball toss for the next two weeks. You do know that you can fix that in like that. You do know that you can make the choice right now to never, ever, ever hit a ball toss that you're not sure about. That have to be a hundred percent. If you're not sure, catch it how many times as coaches. And I think that's such a good sort of example of what we're trying to teach. How many of the coaches that are listening to this go, oh my God, I've got the same player every week, week out. It's that ball toss. Well, at one point you're going to have to have a conversation and say, hey, hey, hey, buddy, this isn't about the toss anymore. This is about, this is about you deciding what you want. If you're not going to get the toss right, how can, how can we, how can you trust yourself and deepen this? Trust yourself and deepen the fifth set when you know you haven't even trusted yourself with under no pressure. Get the toss right with me standing two courts away. So it's things like that. And I think when you get to a certain level and age, I'm going to try and pay back and coach these young coaches to say, have those conversations.

If you're not happy with the way a parent is operating in your project, you know, have the have the courage to go and have a very sensible, very polite conversation about, you know, is this, is this helping, is this helping your player? It makes me think very much. It's very much autonomy coaching, isn't it? Like, you know, just giving them, giving them the power to make these decisions and controlling what they can control. Robert Lansdorf. Absolutely. One of the wonderful, wonderful human beings, wonderful coach, wonderful charismatic. Yeah. I've been seeing a lot of his videos popping up online. And I was just thinking about a big guy, Robert Lansdorf. Yeah. Thank you. Thank you. Last question, and we've probably got about five minutes left. I wish we had two hours and I'm sure anyone watching this would love it two hours, but I'll get in trouble if I don't stick to the, to the timings. But the last question I've got for you is around the art of coaching at the top level, which you already touched on. At the elite level, sort of coaching becomes as much about communication trust like you were saying, as it is rather drills and data. I wonder sometimes people are looking at those sort of, what drills can I do with my players, but actually, what have you learned about building that trust and creating a buy-in with players like Jack and Joe? And how do you adapt your coaching style to suit sort of different personalities and performance demands?

Well, I mean, yeah, there's going to be a difference between all your players, but the difference sort of at the top of the tour level is you know your timeline. So, you know, when you know you've got to play tomorrow, you're playing tomorrow at midday. You know, what we tended to do, especially with Joe, and you know, he's performed pretty well in some big matches over the last few years is and it's needed tinkering with, you know, the scouting report will get done. Almost immediately as soon as you know when, you know, when and who you're playing and that information. So if you like that specific tennis information needs to be somewhere in your brain, needs to be somewhere you need to know where the opponents are going to be serving at the big moments or the likelihood. You need to know obviously what their best returns are, whether they chip a lot of a lot, how close they stand to the net. But this information is something that if you like, needs to be stored and probably a brain surgeon would know this a lot better than I would. It's somewhere in your head, 24 hours before 12 hours before a good a good deal of time before, because what you don't want to do and one of the things that I'm on the team to do is to is to bring the performer out at the right time. With Justin as well, it sounds like when we go right back to the first question when you were, you know, getting them boxing and getting them fighting that all that sort of intuitive.

It will come back to the surface right like all those all those sessions where you're opening the racket face and like and fighting to play first to 10 and doing some boxing and those intuitive moments when they know when to duck or weave out the way or back off. It all just instinctively comes later right and you've installed that from the very beginning through fundamental movement skills and game based activities. Must be very hard to teach that later in life if you haven't had those early years of what you've done. You've already and you've already, you know, you've already put those foundations down. Yeah. Yeah, I think it is difficult to teach it later on but what I found interesting is because I pick up a few players and I try and support a few players along the way or they may have heard that. I can help players perform better and they come to me with almost no, no interaction with me beforehand. And then the impact of a conversation, the impact of telling absolute basics to somebody they need to hear that it's amazing how many basics of fighting and doing your best. And that's all you can do and playing point by point and staying in the moment. It's amazing how much you can teach that over so many years but it still needs reminding. Remember because there's lots of things that go on that I had and we get so distracted but the moment is the most important time and the moment is the only thing that you can also be have any influence over and the moment doesn't define you.
